findings.title: DAP backend debuggee child process leaks on every error path (no Drop/kill guard)
findings.description: run_session spawns lldb-dap (BackendProcess holding std::process::Child) then translates/forwards editor messages. Six bail-out points use `?` (read L241, decode L248, translate L250, encode L251, stdin write/flush L255/L258): any of them returns Err WITHOUT kill()/wait() on backend.child and without joining the backend reader thread. Only the clean stdin-EOF path (L242-245) reaches the drain logic at L264-285. backend.rs:137 comment says the child is 'kept for kill on drop' but no `impl Drop` exists anywhere in buff-dap/src (verified by grep).
findings.root_cause: Cleanup was written as straight-line code after the loop instead of an RAII guard; `?` short-circuits skip it. The 'kill on drop' Drop impl was never implemented despite the comment.
findings.impact: Any protocol error, malformed editor message, or I/O hiccup leaves an orphaned lldb-dap/debuggee process (and a blocked reader thread) per failed session; repeated debug-session failures accumulate zombie processes on the user's machine.
findings.recommendation: Add a session guard struct (or impl Drop for BackendProcess) that kills + waits the child on drop, and use it for all early-return paths; join/abort the reader thread via the guard too.
fix_guide: Wrap backend.child in a Drop guard struct at spawn time in backend.rs
Replace the manual drop(stdin)+wait() sequence with normal scope exit
On the clean path, take the child out of the guard (mem::take) before the existing wait() for the exit-status check
Add an integration test that forces a decode error and asserts no child survives

effort_estimate.breakdown: 30m guard struct + spawn rewiring, 30m clean-path mem::take refactor, 30m leak test

findings.verification_command: Select-String -Path crates\buff-dap\src\*.rs -Pattern 'impl Drop|\.kill\(' ; Select-String -Path crates\buff-dap\src\server.rs -Pattern '\?' | Select-Object -Skip 230 -First 30

confidence.rationale: Code-path reading confirms 6 `?` exits before any kill/wait; grep proves no Drop impl; only normal-EOF path cleans up

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: No allowlist or AGENTS.md entry documents skipping child cleanup; the backend.rs comment itself promises kill-on-drop, making this an unimplemented intention, not a choice
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: buff-dap AGENTS.md (no exemption), root AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md hard rules

findings.title: T24 panic hook is never installed: runtime::init() has zero callers, generated programs and REPL/Jupyter lack it
findings.description: buff-lang-runtime/src/lib.rs:137 documents 'the Buff CLI calls this from generated fn main() startup so user programs get Buff traces transparently'. Workspace-wide grep for `buff_lang_runtime::init(` / `install_panic_hook()` finds only the definition (runtime lib.rs:142), the debug-info crate itself, and `buff backtrace` (commands/backtrace.rs:175). Codegen-rust emits no init call (grep over src + tests snapshots: zero matches), and buff-lang-cli main, buff-repl, and buff-jupyter never install it. The documented auto-hook behavior does not exist; `buff backtrace` is the only manual path.
findings.root_cause: T24 shipped the hook library and the post-mortem `buff backtrace` command, but the codegen/main() injection the runtime docs promise was never wired (or was lost in later refactors), and no test asserts the hook lands in generated code.
findings.impact: User programs panic with raw Rust backtraces instead of the advertised .buff-span traces; REPL/Jupyter panics likewise unmapped. A documented fault-tolerance/debuggability feature is silently dead and docs mislead contributors.
findings.recommendation: Either emit `buff_lang_runtime::init();` at the top of generated fn main() in codegen-rust (with extern_crate_registration adding buff-lang-runtime) or fix the doc to state the hook is opt-in via `buff backtrace`; add a codegen snapshot asserting the init call.

fix_examples.before: // runtime lib.rs:137 doc: 'the Buff CLI calls this from generated fn main() startup'

fix_guide: Add init() prologue emission in codegen-rust main-fn lowering behind the debuginfo choice
Register buff-lang-runtime in extern_crates for that mode
Update runtime lib.rs doc to match implemented behavior either way
Add snapshot test: generated main contains buff_lang_runtime::init()

effort_estimate.breakdown: 45m codegen emission + crate registration, 30m snapshots, 30m docs, 15m CI check

confidence.rationale: Exhaustive workspace grep shows zero init callers; small chance init is injected via a non-obvious path (e.g. inject_profiling), but grep over pipeline/codegen found none

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: Runtime docs themselves frame REPL/Jupyter hook use as MAY (optional), so only the generated-code claim is a violation; that claim is contradicted by code, not by an allowlist
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: runtime AGENTS.md, debug-info AGENTS.md, root AGENTS.md T24 notes

findings.title: SQLite storage performs blocking file I/O directly inside async axum handlers (no spawn_blocking)
findings.description: With BUFF_REGISTRY_DB_PATH set (durable mode, T57), all 22 storage call sites in handlers.rs (publish put_version L447, get_tarball L515, list_versions L545, validate_token L356, ...) execute synchronous rusqlite queries + blob writes while holding the connection Mutex directly on tokio worker threads. Zero occurrences of spawn_blocking in the crate (verified). The registry AGENTS.md explicitly anticipated this: 'A real DB-backed impl can wrap its async ops in tokio::task::spawn_blocking' - the shipped SqliteStorage did not apply that mitigation.
findings.root_cause: Sync Storage trait called from async handlers; SQLite backend added in T57 without the documented spawn_blocking wrapper, so disk-latency queries park tokio workers.
findings.impact: Slow disk or a large tarball publish stalls a tokio worker; concurrent requests queue behind the connection Mutex held for full I/O duration (not the documented nanosecond in-memory case), degrading or stalling the registry under load.
findings.recommendation: Wrap SqliteStorage call sites in tokio::task::spawn_blocking (per-crate AGENTS.md already prescribes the pattern), or make handlers call through a spawn_blocking adapter on AppState when the backend is SQLite.
fix_guide: Add a spawn_blocking helper on AppState used by all handler storage calls
Keep InMemoryStorage on the fast path (skip spawn_blocking for it or accept the tiny cost)
Add a test with a large tarball asserting other requests proceed concurrently

effort_estimate.breakdown: 60m adapter + 22 call sites, 45m error plumbing (JoinError), 45m concurrency test

confidence.rationale: 22 sync call sites verified in async handlers; spawn_blocking absent; only uncertainty is practical latency impact (rusqlite is fast for this dataset)

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: AGENTS.md documents the in-memory nanosecond-hold as deliberate, but explicitly points to spawn_blocking for DB backends - the shipped SQLite path contradicts the documented mitigation, so it is not a documented choice

findings.title: buff-resilience (retry/circuit-breaker) has zero consumers; retry logic re-implemented in buff-jobs instead
findings.description: Workspace-wide scan of crates/*/Cargo.toml finds buff-resilience referenced ONLY by its own manifest; no crate depends on it and no src file imports buff_resilience (grep across crates/*/src: zero). Meanwhile buff-http-client performs single-shot requests (no retry integration, P0.17 covers timeouts only), and buff-jobs ships its own independent backoff implementation (buff-jobs/src/backoff.rs, ~11 sites) duplicating exponential-backoff semantics. The v1.16 flagship fault-tolerance crate is effectively dead code shipped to users.
findings.root_cause: Wave-4 framework crates were built as standalone MVPs (per buff-image T9 'MVP first, wiring second' precedent) and the wiring follow-up for resilience never happened.
findings.impact: Shipped surface lacks integrated retry/circuit-breaking: user HTTP calls fail hard on transient errors, jobs and resilience drift apart (two backoff implementations to maintain), and the advertised SDK 2.0 resilience story is not real.
findings.recommendation: Wire buff-http-client to an optional retry policy built on buff_resilience (or document the crate as standalone-only in root AGENTS.md), and have buff-jobs consume buff_resilience backoff to collapse the duplication.

fix_examples.before:
// buff-jobs/src/backoff.rs - local exponential backoff impl
// buff-http-client send(): client.execute(req).await?  // no retry
fix_examples.after:
// buff-http-client: pub fn retry(mut self, policy: buff_resilience::RetryPolicy) -> Self
// send loop: for attempt in policy.attempts() { match send_once().await { Ok(v)=>return Ok(v), Err(e) if !policy.should_retry(&e)=>return Err(e), _=>continue } }

fix_guide: Add buff-resilience dep to buff-http-client and expose a retry(policy) builder
Replace buff-jobs backoff internals with buff_resilience equivalents (keep public API)
Add root AGENTS.md note documenting the integration
Add integration test: flaky endpoint retried to success
findings.technology: Rust workspace framework crates (buff-resilience, buff-http-client, buff-jobs)

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: Standalone-MVP framing exists for cache/pubsub but root AGENTS.md lists buff-resilience as shipped SDK surface without any standalone-only caveat; absence of consumers is objective
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: AGENTS.md v1.16 wave notes, buff-cache/buff-pubsub AGENTS.md DEFERRED precedent sections
convention_files_checked: crates/buff-resilience/AGENTS.md (none found at crate root - checked)

findings.title: Registry server lacks graceful shutdown (axum::serve without with_graceful_shutdown)
findings.description: main.rs:68 runs `axum::serve(listener, app(state)).await?` with no with_graceful_shutdown wiring, unlike the ui_dev server in the same workspace (buff-lang-cli/src/ui_dev/mod.rs:110-116 which uses tokio::signal + with_graceful_shutdown and explicitly documents draining in-flight requests). On SIGTERM/Ctrl+C the process dies mid-request; with the T57 durable SQLite backend this can abandon an in-flight publish transaction.
findings.root_cause: Binary written as a minimal v1.6 smoke entry ('exists primarily to confirm the crate builds') and never upgraded when durable SQLite storage made in-flight request loss meaningful.
findings.impact: Deploys/restarts cut off active publishes and downloads; interrupted SQLite writes rely solely on journaling for recovery; inconsistent with the workspace's own ui_dev precedent.
findings.recommendation: Mirror ui_dev: tokio::signal::ctrl_c + with_graceful_shutdown so axum drains in-flight requests before exit.
fix_guide: Add with_graceful_shutdown with ctrl_c (+ SIGTERM via tokio::signal::unix on non-Windows)
Log 'shutting down, draining...' to stderr
Optionally add a smoke test asserting the app() router still builds (behavior unchanged)

confidence.rationale: Direct read of the 70-line main.rs; in-workspace contrast case verified

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: AGENTS.md documents the binary as a minimal entry point, which is a partial deliberate-choice defense; severity kept low for that reason, but the SQLite durable mode added later changed the calculus
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: buff-registry AGENTS.md ('binary entry NOT exercised by tests; exists to prove the crate builds')

findings.title: Kernelspec advertises interrupt_mode='signal' but the kernel has no SIGINT handler - interrupt kills the kernel
findings.description: KERNEL_INTERRUPT_MODE = "signal" (kernelspec.rs:50) tells Jupyter to interrupt via SIGINT (Unix) / CTRL_BREAK_EVENT (Windows). The Rust kernel process installs no signal handler (grep 'interrupt|SIGINT' in buff-jupyter/src: only the ACK-only interrupt_request at kernel.rs:250-255, documented as 'ack only, cancellation lands in T129c+'). With the OS default disposition, that signal terminates the whole kernel process - so 'Interrupt kernel' in Jupyter kills the session (losing all cross-cell state) rather than stopping the running cell.
findings.root_cause: T129a shipped ACK-only interrupts and chose the default 'signal' mode without either honoring signals or declaring 'message' mode; the documented limitation covers interrupt_request handling but not the kernel-death consequence of signal mode.
findings.impact: Users interrupting a long cell lose the entire session state; on Windows, CTRL_BREAK_EVENT emulation may also hard-exit. Documented gap understates the blast radius.
findings.recommendation: Short term: install a SIGINT handler that sets a cancellation flag checked between eval steps (or between rustc-spawn phases); alternatively document 'Interrupt kernel terminates this kernel in v1.7' in lib.rs and kernelspec docs until T129c lands.

fix_examples.before: pub const KERNEL_INTERRUPT_MODE: &str = "signal"; // no handler installed anywhere

fix_guide: Add a process-wide AtomicBool cancellation flag
Install signal handler (ctrlc crate or tokio::signal) in run_kernel
Check the flag between eval/rustc phases and emit an 'interrupted' error status
Document the interim behavior in kernel.rs module docs
findings.technology: Jupyter kernel protocol v5, zeromq 0.4, tokio (buff-jupyter)

confidence.rationale: ACK-only handling and signal-mode advertising are verified; exact OS-level kill behavior inferred from default signal dispositions (not runtime-tested)

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: interrupt_request ACK-only is a documented deliberate T129a limitation (FP per rules); the finding is narrowed to the undocumented signal-mode/kernel-death mismatch, which no convention file covers
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: buff-jupyter AGENTS.md, kernel.rs module docs (T129a/c notes)

findings.title: web3 flattens provider error chains via map_err(|e| e.to_string())
findings.description: get_chainid (lib.rs:580) and its sibling call (586) convert typed provider errors with `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())?`, discarding the error chain (RPC method, provider type, source cause) in violation of the project's thiserror/`#[from]` error-propagation convention. This is one of only two genuine map_err-loss sites in non-test src (the rest are codegen templates that intentionally emit this pattern into USER programs, e.g. instance_fns_extra.rs:1313 for Buff's `validate` lowering - by design, not a repo defect).
findings.root_cause: Convenience String error in the web3 public API instead of a thiserror enum with #[from] over the provider/transports error types.
findings.impact: Users debugging failed RPC calls see only a Display string with no source chain; programmatic matching on failure kinds (timeout vs revert vs connection) is impossible.
findings.recommendation: Introduce Web3Error (thiserror) with #[from] on the provider error and keep the chain; map to buff_lang_error variants per CONTRIBUTING conventions.
fix_guide: Add Web3Error thiserror enum with #[from] variants
Replace the two to_string() map_errs with bare `?`
Keep existing String-returning helpers as wrappers if the public API must stay stable

effort_estimate.breakdown: 45m enum design, 20m two call sites, 25m tests

confidence.rationale: Both sites read in context; error type of surrounding fn returns String-based error, so chain loss is certain

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: No convention or allowlist documents String-flattening as acceptable; the similar codegen-emitted pattern was excluded as by-design language semantics
fp_risk_self_assessment.verified_against_conventions: CONTRIBUTING.md hard rules (thiserror derive, map to buff_lang_error), root AGENTS.md

All 8 exceptions match scripts/check-unwrap-ban.ps1 allowlist exactly.
